summary: SYNESTHESIA turns real NASA Earth data (Earth Information Center visualizations and NASA POWER weather records) into sound you can trace back to its source. You can play any of the 9 Earth Information Center visualizations, hear a place’s weather, history and anomalies against its 2001–2020 normal, and get a regional soundscape with findings computed from the data. It also includes the Amazon 2024 drought case study and an ear-only Listening Test.
details:
SYNESTHESIA turns real NASA Earth data into sound you can trace back to its source. Our challenge was The Earth Information Jukebox.

What it does:

- Jukebox: pick one of the nine Earth Information Center visualizations and hear it. The app reads each frame's brightness, warmth and contrast, and you can drag a "hand" across the image to play the pixels under the pointer.

- Hear Earth: pick any place and dates to hear NASA POWER daily measurements as one soundscape. Temperature is pitch, rain is percussion, wind is loudness, humidity is texture, pressure is vibrato and cloud adds voices. Unusual values ring a bell.

- History and Anomalies: a place's monthly record since 1981, played against its 2001-2020 normal, and a 48-point global grid that rings when a day is unusual.

- Earth Listening Intelligence: samples a whole region (for example the Indian Ocean) and plays it as one soundscape. Alongside the sound it lists findings computed from the data: records, trends, robust z-scores and runs. Each finding links to its numbers, grid points and NASA requests.

- Case study: finds the Amazon's August-November 2024 heat-and-drought event and lets you hear it against a quiet reference year before revealing four synced charts.

- Listening Test: an ear-only experiment with real NASA clips that checks whether people can actually hear anomalies.

Benefits and impact: blind and low-vision people, students and the public can explore climate data by ear, not only through charts. Every note is traceable. A live caption and a Trace panel show the exact measurement behind each sound, so the result is evidence, not decoration. It works from the keyboard and has high-contrast and reduced-motion modes.

Tools: TypeScript, React, Vite and the Web Audio API on the front end. Python and FastAPI run a small data proxy on the back end. Data comes from NASA POWER, NASA SVS / Earth Information Center visualizations and NASA GIBS Blue Marble imagery. Vitest, pytest and Playwright run the tests.

What makes it creative: it works like a scientific instrument. One soundscape carries several variables at once, so you can hear heat, drought and wind arrive together where a reader would otherwise compare four charts.

What we considered: scientific honesty (fixed, documented mappings, no claims about causes, missing data shown as missing), accessibility, listenability (musical scales, and a compressor so stacked notes don't distort) and validation (a pre-specified listening study design).

Code: https://github.com/yashvardhan9009/synesthesia
